title: Agglomeration Economy Dynamics and Demand Spillovers:  Restaurant Week Effect on Participants’ Neighbors
authors: Roxanne Jaffe (Vanderbilt University)
abstract: Agglomeration economies generate benefits for agglomerated firms. How benefits propagate through an agglomeration is unclear because agglomerations are composed of multiple firms and each firm engages in various activities that might have spillover implications for neighbors. To observe this propagation and identify underlying mechanisms, we leverage some firms taking a specific strategic action that generates benefits for themselves that might spill over to neighbors. Focusing on demand-side (vs. supply-side) agglomeration benefits, we expect that neighbors will benefit more when geographically closer to the action-taking firms (due to lower customer search costs) or when selling similar goods to the action-taking firms (due to what customers the strategic action attracts), but benefit less when both geographically closer and selling similar goods (due to localized competition). Using a quasi-natural experiment featuring establishment-level micro-geographic data of restaurants participating in “Restaurant Week” in Washington DC (an event to stimulate demand), we find that Restaurant Week participants’ neighbors experience heightened demand for several weeks after Restaurant Week. Consistent with our expectations: neighbors benefit more when geographically closer or if selling similar goods to Restaurant Week participants. But the benefit for neighbors selling similar goods is delayed a couple weeks, which is consistent with localized competition initially offsetting spillover benefits. Our results demonstrate how firms taking specific strategic action can lead to spillovers propagating throughout an agglomeration, and how overlapping mechanisms determine who benefits and how much.

title: The Buc-ee’s Effect: Measuring the impact of shopping tourism on local economies
authors: Christopher Smith (University of Southern Mississippi)
abstract: The Buc-ee’s gas station and convenience store chain has recently undertaken a campaign of expansion outside of its home state of Texas. As it opens new locations, some observers have suggested the potential for a unique “Buc-ee’s effect” on local economies due to the company’s dedicated customer base. This paper studies point-of-interest visitation data to measure local effects from the opening of Buc-ee’s branch stores from 2019-2025.

title: How Coopetition Dynamics Change as Industries Mature: Evidence from the U.S. Craft Brewing Industry
authors: Hyunsoo Kim (New York University); J.P. Eggers (New York University)
abstract: We explore how coopetitive preferences change as an industry matures by examining both the macro trends around within-industry collaboration formation and the micro behaviors of partner selection across multiple dimensions of strategic similarity in the U.S. craft brewing industry. Abductively studying multi-brewery collaboration beers from 2007 to 2023,  we find that the rate of coopetition formation increases even as the industry matures. The nature of partner selection, however, fundamentally shifts in two theoretically important ways. First, firms prefer to buffer increasing competitive pressures by dramatically reducing partner similarity on one dimension while maximizing it on another, presumably to improve value creation opportunities. This highlights the strategic importance of multi-attribute trade-off management. Second, high-status incumbents abandon the collectivist "rising tide" logics in favor of self-preservation, clustering with highly similar local peers to pull up the ladder behind them in ways that reduce entry and accelerate competitor exits.

title: Optimizing Vessel Transit Efficiency in the Welland Canal: A Simulation-Based Approach to Lock Congestion
authors: Ashesh Sinha (West Virginia University); John Saldanha (West Virginia University)
abstract: This research investigates maritime congestion patterns within the Welland Canal, a critical artery of the St. Lawrence Seaway transporting over 40 million tons of cargo annually comprising of essential commodities, including grain, iron ore, and manufacturing materials. While the canal utilizes a system of eight locks, the configuration of single (one-way) locks creates significant bottlenecks compared to the twinned (two-way) sections. Utilizing a discrete-event simulation model, this study evaluates vessel speed optimization strategies—specifically when ships should accelerate or decelerate—to minimize transit delays. Furthermore, the research explores operational flexibility within the twinned locks, assessing the impact of unidirectional 'double-flow' scheduling to alleviate peak congestion. The results of this research have the potential to improve the flow of vessels and cargo through the Welland Canal lock system as well as reduce the idling and concomitant fuel consumption associated with vessels queueing to enter the canal.

title: From Bribes to Bytes: How Has Fraud Evolved in the U.S. Transportation Sector Projects?
authors: Young Kwak (George Washington University); Manisha Bhetwal (George Washington University); Sureewan  Jampathong (George Washington University)
abstract: The United States transportation infrastructure sector is currently navigating a period of historic capital expansion, a context that historical data suggests is frequently correlated with opportunistic behavior and systemic fraud. This study presents a longitudinal analysis of 2,028 confirmed Department of Transportation (DOT) violations spanning from 1998 to 2025. Transitioning beyond traditional statistical methods, this research employs Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) to deconstruct the linguistic architecture of fraud descriptions, enabling a high-precision classification of latent project governance failures. The analysis reveals a distinct "Digital Crossover," where physical bribery and safety non-compliance have been superseded by digital wire fraud and complex "pass-through" schemes involving Disadvantaged Business Enterprises (DBE). Furthermore, semantic clustering identifies five major frauds, with "DBE Shell Games" and "Moving Hostage Schemes" carrying the highest financial severity. The paper prposes a transition from retrospective auditing to real-time, blockchain-enabled "Verify-then-Pay" frameworks to close the verification gap in project delivery.

title: ESG Challenges in Large-scale Infrastructure Projects
authors: Sun Kim (Michigan State University); Sriram Narayanan (Michigan State University)
abstract:
Large-scale infrastructure projects are critical for economic development and societal well-being, with global spending on infrastructure accounting for more than 10% of the world GDP. These projects are unique in nature in terms of design and location, technically complicated and large in scale, and thus have great level of impact on various stakeholders. While these projects are notorious for their frequent cost overruns and delays, the large physical nature makes such projects especially susceptible to various sustainability challenges.

While various factors have been studied extensively as drivers of project performance, sustainability challenges, specifically, the role of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) risks remains largely underexplored in operations management literature. This study investigates ESG risks in large-scale infrastructure projects by examining ESG-related challenges and risks over the life cycle of projects.

We analyze 280 large-scale infrastructure projects from the World Bank, spanning transportation, water, and energy sectors across 64 countries. We first develop a comprehensive project-related ESG taxonomy through text analysis using text data obtained from ESG-related documents and project documents from the World Bank. Using the identified ESG terms, we measure intensity of ESG-related risks at the point of project planning and after completion of the projects. By comparing project appraisal documents with completion reports, we identify which ESG risks are likely to be anticipated during planning versus those that emerge over the project's implementation and examine how these emergent challenges influence project performance outcomes.

This study contributes to operations management by investigating an underexplored intersection of infrastructure project management and sustainability and showing ESG-related factors as important drivers of project performance.

title: Volume or Depth? Operational Pathways to Federal Funding Success in Nonprofits
authors: Telesilla Kotsi (The Ohio State University); Gloria Urrea (University of Colorado Boulder); Sebastian Villa (University of Colorado Boulder)
abstract:
Project grants and cooperative agreements constitute nearly one-third of total government funding for nonprofit organizations (NPOs) in the U.S. However, given frequent funding reductions, NPOs face increasing pressure to configure their operational competencies to match the distinct requirements of federal agencies. Because project grants require standardized competencies while cooperative agreements demand collaborative, agency-specific ones, NPOs must strategically choose between two operational pathways: volume (pursuing funding across multiple agencies) or depth (building repetitive funding interactions with the same agency). This study examines how these pathways shape NPOs' ability to signal the required competencies to secure future federal funding.
We assemble a unique longitudinal dataset of 7,845 federal awards totaling $15.8 billion to 1,925 NPOs from 2017–2024 and apply Relational Event Models to capture the temporal dependence among sequential funding events. Our results show that the success of an NPO’s operational pathway depends critically on the funding mechanism. Depth pathways in project grants strengthen relationships with federal agencies and increase the likelihood of securing both awards types (project grants and cooperative agreements) by up to 2.5%. In contrast, pursuing a volume pathway in project grants significantly reduces success in cooperative agreements by 18.7%, suggesting that agencies may interpret this experience as a lack of collaborative capacity. Furthermore, while both pathways in cooperative agreements produce cross-agency learning and reputational spillovers, volume proves especially effective for NPOs with this experience, enhancing access to both awards types by up to 11.8%. Our findings highlight strategic trade-offs in managing government funding. For NPO leaders, the optimal funding strategy depends on existing experience: depth is most effective for organizations with project grant histories, while volume better serves those experienced in cooperative agreements. For federal program officers, funding histories should be interpreted relative to the award being evaluated. Prior cooperative agreement experience signals collaborative readiness in ways that project grant experience does not.

title: Navigating Green Innovation and Industrial Resilience: Policy Pathways for Low-Carbon Transformation under Technological and Policy Uncertainty
authors: Shah Fahad (Leshan Normal University)
abstract: In an era marked by rapid technological disruption, climate imperatives, and increasingly proactive policy regimes, firms and industries face complex uncertainties that influence innovation trajectories and competitive dynamics. This study investigates how green innovation interacts with public policy to shape industrial performance and resilience, focusing on the transition to low-carbon pathways in energy-intensive sectors. Drawing on a mixed-methods framework, we combine quantitative analysis of firm-level innovation and emissions data with qualitative evidence from industry case studies to identify mechanisms through which policy instruments such as carbon pricing, regulatory standards, and innovation subsidies modulate firms’ strategic responses. Our findings reveal that enabling policy frameworks can significantly enhance the diffusion of green technologies, while industry-specific institutional capacities mediate the effectiveness of these interventions. By highlighting the interplay of innovation, policy design, and firm behavior in uncertain environments, this research offers actionable insights for policymakers and industry leaders seeking to accelerate sustainable industrial transformation.

title: The Lone Rancher: Digital and AI-Mediated Governance in Upstream Cattle Production
authors: Darcy Fudge (Sacramento State); Steven Hyde (Boise State); Chad Coffman (Boise State)
abstract:
How do digital and AI-mediated technologies reshape informal organizing in upstream industry contexts? We examine this question through a qualitative study of the U.S. cattle ranching industry, focusing on how ranchers coordinate land, labor, and animals. Although beef is priced and traded in well-developed markets, upstream activities in cattle ranching have historically been coordinated through informal organizing, including relational ties, local knowledge, and negotiated discretion among ranchers, workers, market intermediaries, and public land managers. Prior technological change in the industry has centered on genetics, animal health, and quality assessment, leaving these informal organizing arrangements largely intact. In contrast, recent advances in GPS-enabled headcollars, drones, and remote monitoring technologies, however, introduce new forms of visibility and control into this land-intensive industry.

Drawing on extensive interview data, including ranch owners, ranch hands, livestock auction operators, agricultural extension officers, veterinarians, and participants with experience interacting with the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), we analyze how digital monitoring technologies reconfigure informal organizing in cattle ranching. Our findings describe a shift from community-based forms of informal organizing, characterized by shared norms, interpersonal trust, and face-to-face coordination, toward more centralized and market-like arrangements in which authority is enacted through data, metrics, and remote oversight. These technologies enable individual ranchers to manage larger herds with fewer workers while reducing reliance on ongoing traditions involving relational coordination with local networks, intermediaries, and land managers. We conceptualize this transformation as a movement from relationally embedded organizing toward data-mediated control, altering how authority is exercised and how coordination is achieved across loosely coupled actors. This shift situates cattle ranching within a digital and AI-mediated era of industry governance and highlights how technological change reshapes informal organizing in settings traditionally governed through social relations.

title: Supply Chain Interventions by States Promoting the Competitive Viability of their Dairy Producers Facing Federal Regulations that Affect Distribution Costs: The Case of West Virginia
authors: Ashesh Sinha (West Virginia University); John Saldanha (West Virginia University); Molly Hughes (West Virginia University)
abstract: Federal Milk Marketing Orders (FMMO) regulate the orderly flow of milk from dairy farmers (producers) to market and set milk prices for producers in the United States (U.S.). The 2000 FMMO revisions appear to have mixed effects on U.S. states’ milk production. Some states experienced growth while others, such as West Virginia (WV), experienced contraction. The June 2025 revisions prompted the question, how can states intervene to enhance the competitive viability of their dairy industry? To answer this question we develop a multi-period two-echelon vehicle-routing problem mixed integer linear program (MILP) with inventory. Our MILP exploits network scale economies and transportation density economies to grow WV producers' market extent and leverage the higher prices in the 2025 revisions. We use the MILP as a framework to develop several policy scenario analyses to promote the competitive viability of WV producers. The WV Legislature authorized the West Virginia Department of Agriculture (WVDA) to assist small dairy producers, allowing WVDA to act on our recommendations. We discuss our contributions to (1) the two-echelon VRP literature, (2) theory at the intersection of public policy and supply chain management, and (3) the agricultural economics literature. We present practical implications for policy makers and dairy professionals including limitations of our research, which we hope spurs future research.

title: Embedded Greenhouse Gas Emissions in U.S. Soybean and Soybean Meal Trade and Sustainability Implications for Global Supply Chains
authors: Aurup Ratan Dhar (Institute on the Environment, University of Minnesota); Nathaniel Springer (Institute on the Environment, University of Minnesota); Jinsu  Hong (Department of Animal Science, University of Minnesota); Pedro E. Urriola (Department of Animal Science, University of Minnesota); Mary  Ollenburger (Institute on the Environment, University of Minnesota); Jennifer  Schmitt (Institute on the Environment, University of Minnesota); Gerald C.  Shurson (Department of Animal Science, University of Minnesota)
abstract:
Global soybean and soybean meal (SBM) markets play a critical role in food, feed, and bioenergy systems, yet their environmental impacts vary widely across production regions and supply-chain pathways. This study quantified the cradle-to-market greenhouse gas (GHG) emission intensities for U.S. soybean and SBM exports in 2023 using the Food System Supply-Chain Sustainability (FoodS³) model, integrating county-level soybean production and crushing data, land-use change (LUC) and carbon emissions, and international trade flows.
Results showed that U.S. soybean exports had an average cradle-to-market emission intensity of 1.49 kgCO₂e kg⁻¹, while SBM exports averaged 1.12 kgCO₂e kg⁻¹, with production and LUC accounting for more than 80% of total emissions. Transport and processing contributed relatively little compared with upstream production processes. Emission intensities varied by several-fold across export corridors and destination markets, driven primarily by whether sourcing counties reflect long-established cropland or recent agricultural expansion. Because routing through specific ports and soybean crushers aggregates upstream emissions heterogeneity, national averages mask substantial within-country variation that is consequential for buyers, policymakers, and downstream industries.
A case study of SBM-derived crude protein embedded in exported pork diets demonstrated that relative to U.S. pork produced with U.S. SBM, feed-related GHG emissions were approximately 13× higher for Brazil-based pork produced with domestic SBM, 8× higher for China-based pork produced with domestic SBM, and 4× higher for China-based pork produced with imported U.S. SBM. Overall, the analysis highlighted the importance of spatially explicit supply-chain GHG accounting to support climate-aligned trade, procurement, and biofuel expansion policies in global agri-food systems.

title: Children Before Profits: Constraining Private Equity Profiteering to Advance Child Care as a Public Good
authors: Audrey Stienon (Open Markets Institute)
abstract:
The Open Markets Institute and National Women’s Law Center published the original “Children Before Profits” report in June 2024, and will be publishing a follow-up report “Children Before Profits in the States” in January 2026. The crux of our presentation to ISA will draw from the original report — but will include the more up-to-date examples and policy discussions from the more recent paper. 

The findings of this research have been shared to diverse policymakers and child care advocates, but in presenting at the ISA conference, we hope to have the opportunity to discuss not only our policy recommendations, but also our research and analytical methodology, and our thoughts about how this paper ties into broader debates about the nature and scope of industrial policy.

This paper builds on existing research of the harms that private equity firms have caused in diverse sectors of the economy by exploring potential threats that private equity could pose to other child care industry stakeholders, including workers, families, and small business owners. It then identifies policy opportunities to address these risks (with the 2026 follow-up paper fleshing out these opportunities at the state and local level). 

An overarching hypothesis of this project is that private equity makes for a good case study for the type of firms that prioritize profit maximization over any other goals, and that therefore, by understanding the ways that private equity behaves in a sector like child care, policymakers can build guardrails to align the activities of all types of profit-maximizing firms with broader social priorities, like access and affordability.

As background for this paper, we studied the market structure and firm business models for the private equity, child care, and other industries that had experienced high levels of private equity investment (e.g. retail, nursing homes, hospice care). This allowed us to identify structural similarities between the firms and markets of the child care industry, and those of other sectors that were harmed by private equity profit-maximizing tactics. From there, we could hypothesize about the risks that private equity activity posed to child care markets, and suggest policy interventions to address these risks.

We chose to study the child care industry because we believed that underlying market failures of this sector (i.e. under-funded, and thus largely unprofitable for providers) had kept private equity out of this market. Advocates were concerned that new campaigns to increase public funding for child care could increase private equity interest in this space. Our policy recommendations were intended to encourage policymakers to act preemptively in addressing potential risks.

We were also interested in using this project to broaden the scope of industrial policy discussions. This paper was an experiment in developing a well-researched industrial policy strategy for a sector that is non-import-competing, requires improvements in neither innovation nor global competitiveness, and is largely dependent on public funding. Child care is a socially critical service, and many of the market challenges facing this sector (under-supply, poor job quality, unaffordability) are the same as other sectors targeted by industrial policy strategies. Furthermore, we wanted to use this paper as a case study for the ways that financial sector capture can interrupt other industrial strategy priorities — a challenge that we argue is increasingly relevant across all sectors.

title: Strategic Focus: Evidence from Private Equity Transactions in US Power Generation Sector
authors: Haiyang Zhang (Harvard Business School)
abstract: Firms aiming to scale often risk unproductive expansions in scope, resulting in diminished focus on core operations and deteriorating performance. This paper exploits the setting of private equity (PE) ownership in the U.S. power generation sector to empirically demonstrate that organizations can achieve “scale without scope,” thereby improving asset-level productivity. Matching high-frequency production data with a decade of transaction records, I find that PE-acquired generating assets improve their heat rate—a direct measure of efficiency—by approximately 2% within five years post-acquisition and about 5% over longer horizons. These efficiency gains emerge from a strategic focus mechanism, the concentration of resources at scale on a narrower set of core generating technologies. Importantly, this is distinct from the traditional learning curve effects: the accumulated depth of experience does not by itself result in better performance; instead, this research supports a contingent view of experience. The value of operational experience is contingent on the organizational context in which it is deployed. In focused organizations, the same depth of experience appears to create greater performance improvements than in diversified ones, suggesting that the returns to experience are not fixed but are shaped by ownership-enabled strategic decisions. Under this frame-work, PE firms can be understood not just as asset owners but as “focus enablers,” organizations that create the conditions under which accumulated experience can be effectively deployed. Beyond conventional PE levers, PE ownership enables an additional value creation mechanism by strategically focusing on core technologies to amplify the returns to experience.

title: Coordinating Market Actors for the Public Good: Competition Policy as the Industrial Policy of Democratic Economic Governance
authors: Audrey Stienon (Open Markets Institute)
abstract:
We start with the premise that industrial policy refers to the mechanisms that governments use to shape markets in the pursuit of a specific outcome, and that these policies are critical to governments' ability to initiate and guide change in the economy. Building on this premise, our paper analyzes the ways that industrial policy strategies can be undermined by market actors’ attempts to unfairly capture or distort markets, and discusses how competition laws, institutions, and policy frameworks have been used in the U.S. to strengthen democratic economic governance, and thereby enable other industrial policy successes. 

Our overarching argument is that democratic economic governance should be an explicit goal of governments’ industrial policy strategies given that it is a prerequisite for achieving other industrial policy priorities, and that competition policies are critical to achieving this goal. 

We start by looking directly industrial policies intended to achieve the goals most often associated with competition policy: addressing the consequences of monopolization and unfair market practices. In these cases, competition policy is clearly the preferred form of industrial policy mechanism, but we also review how other industrial policy tactics can be used to achieve similar outcomes.

Second, we discuss industrial strategies intended to prevent incumbent firms from becoming barriers to change—such as when they restrict innovation, block the entry of new businesses, or otherwise slow the development of new industries. Practices like killer acquisitions, refusals to deal, or exclusive dealing arrangements can undercut new competitors—and sit squarely within the regulatory mandate of antitrust laws.

Third, we look at policy strategies for preventing the incumbents of one industry from leveraging their market power to capture the gains of new or adjacent industries that are the target of governments’ industrial policy campaigns. Here, we discuss the use of industry-specific safeguards, common carriage obligations, and guardrails against financial sector capture.

Fourth, we review strategies for ensuring that the beneficiaries of industrial policies do not themselves use public support to unfairly capture the gains of their own industries, or establish themselves as the barriers to future change. We discuss the importance of integrating competition policy mechanisms into industrial strategies from the onset, and of structuring industrial policies to distribute public support fairly to all market actors in a given sector.

Finally, we look at international markets where, we argue, the monopolistic actors are countries rather than companies. We look at the supply chain risks of geographically concentrated production, and the geopolitical risks of countries weaponizing chokepoints. Here, countries’ classic industrial strategies for building up new industries mirror competition policy strategies for strengthening competitors to monopolist firms. 

This paper was published in the May 2025 issue of the Competition Policy International Antitrust Chronicle, but has not yet been presented at a conference. The authors are building on these ideas in their current research and policy advocacy, and so welcome the opportunity to share our thinking with, and receive input and feedback from the ISA community.

title: Responding to Polycrisis: Industrial Relations and Strategic Action in the German automotive industry
authors: Alexander Bendel (University of Duisburg-Essen); Thomas Bendel (University of Duisburg-Essen)
abstract:
The German automotive industry is currently facing a profound transformation process. A key challenge is the transition to electromobility, which requires substantial investments in new technologies, batteries, and software. At the same time, demand for electric vehicles and political framework conditions remain uncertain, making planning and profitability difficult.  Global competitive pressure has also increased significantly, particularly from Chinese manufacturers, which are technologically advanced in electric vehicles and produce them at low cost. In addition, high production costs in Germany, such as energy prices and labor costs, are weighing on competitiveness. This leads to cost-cutting programs, adjustments in production and job losses. The structural transformation is also reshaping the labor market, as traditional jobs disappear and new skills are required.
In this paper, we explore how the actors within Germany’s system of industrial relations are responding to these challenges, which approaches and strategies they develop, what kinds of labour conflicts arise, and what impact restructuring has on labour regulation. Our analysis is based on case studies of companies in the automotive industry as well as an investigation of industry-level collective bargaining and political lobbying by the collective associations of labour and capital. The core questions we will tackle are: (1) How do works councils react to the polycrisis in their interactions and negotiations with management? (2) What instruments of collective bargaining that cope with these transformations are developed by trade unions and employers’ associations? (3) What demands do the collective actors address to the state and how far do they cooperate in doing this? Based on these questions, we will try to assess the challenges these developments pose for German industrial relations as a whole, given that the automotive industry still forms the backbone of the German model of partnership and corporatism in industrial relations. 
The paper is based on findings from the project ‘Digital and Ecological Transformations in the Regulatory Environment of Labour Relations,’ funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG).

title: Government Capital, Innovation, and Industrial Upgrading: Evidence from the Low-Altitude Economy
authors: Shunru Chen (Jinan University); Feng Tao (Jinan University)
abstract:
Purpose: The low-altitude economy has recently emerged as a pivotal component of strategic emerging industries, playing an increasingly important role in driving innovation-led growth and industrial upgrading. Against this backdrop, this study seeks to examine the role of government guidance funds in shaping the development of emerging industries, with particular emphasis on the mechanisms through which public capital influences firms’ innovation activities and long-term growth trajectories.

Design/methodology/approach: Drawing on institutional economics and Schumpeterian innovation theory, this study constructs an analytical framework to investigate the impact of government guidance funds on the development of low-altitude economy enterprises. Using a panel dataset of listed firms engaged in low-altitude economic activities from 2003 to 2024, the study employs Difference-in-Differences (DID), Propensity Score Matching–Difference-in-Differences (PSM-DID), and Double/Debiased Machine Learning (DDML) methods to identify causal effects and mitigate potential endogeneity and selection bias.

Findings: The empirical results indicate that government guidance funds significantly promote the development of low-altitude economy enterprises. Mechanism analysis shows that this effect operates primarily through alleviating firms’ financing constraints and enhancing their internal capital accumulation capacity, thereby strengthening innovation incentives and supporting sustained investment in research and production. By facilitating capital inflows and improving resource allocation efficiency, government guidance funds contribute to the formation and expansion of emerging industrial clusters. The findings remain robust across multiple specifications and robustness checks.

Originality/value: This study contributes to the literature in three main ways. First, it extends existing research on government guidance funds by focusing on the low-altitude economy, an emerging industry that has received limited empirical attention. Second, by integrating Schumpeterian innovation theory with firm-level evidence, the study reveals the micro-level mechanisms through which public capital promotes industrial evolution. Third, the application of DDML enhances causal identification and provides a rigorous empirical framework for evaluating the effectiveness of government-led industrial policies. The findings offer valuable policy implications for optimizing government guidance funds and fostering sustainable development in strategic emerging industries.

title: Who Really Knows How Many Workers and Firms Are in An Industry?
authors: Andrew Reamer (George Washington University)
abstract: Federal economic statistics by NAICS code are a key input of numerous scholarly studies of individual industries. These data are generated through two registers of the nation's business establishments, each classified by a NAICS code. One register is maintained by the Census Bureau and one by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Unfortunately, federal law prevents these two registers from being synchronized; as a result, the Census Bureau's count of establishments and employees in one NAICS code can vary substantially from the BLS count for the same industry. This disparity can raise questions about the solidity of a substantial proportion of scholarly industry studies. This paper describes the extent of and reasons for such disparities, recent efforts to reduce or eliminate these disparities, and policy options to do so going forward.

title: Regulatory Reform and Market Evolution in the Spectrum Commons
authors: Haiyang Zhang (Harvard Business School); Shane Greenstein (Harvard Business School); Roberto Fontana (University of Pavia); Do Yoon Kim (Boston College)
abstract: How does a decline in regulatory frictions shape innovation and competition in technology markets—and who benefits most from such reforms? This study examines the Federal Communications Commission’s transformation of wireless device regulation between 1997 and 2001, which reduced certification delays, delegated compliance testing to private bodies, and expanded access to unlicensed spectrum. Using administrative records covering nearly 200,000 equipment authorization applications from 1990 to 2015, we analyze how reductions in procedural costs affected product introduction, firm entry and survival patterns, and competitive dynamics. We document a distinctive pattern of market evolution. Following the reforms, regulatory processing times fell sharply, coinciding with a sustained expansion in product introduction and firm participation, particularly in unlicensed spectrum applications. This expansion was driven disproportionately by new entrants, who accounted for most growth in product variety and experimentation across emerging categories. At the same time, established firms retained survival advantages and remained dominant in technically complex product categories. The coexistence of widespread entrant-led experimentation and incumbent persistence is difficult to reconcile with strong forms of regulatory capture, which would predict disproportionate gains for established firms. Taken together, the findings identify a hybrid competitive regime in which regulatory reform broadens access and experimentation without eliminating capability-based advantages. These results inform contemporary debates on privatized certification, commons governance, and the design of regulatory institutions for emerging technologies.

title: Dynamic Competition in Networked Markets: Evidence from US Broadband
authors: Jennifer Zou (Harvard University)
abstract: This paper examines how regulatory policies can promote sustainable entry in US broadband. I develop a dynamic spatial competition model that endogenizes market structure, product differentiation, and capacity investment. On the demand side, households differ in internet preferences by demographics; on the supply side, firms set prices and speeds in a static game subject to capacity constraints, and make dynamic expansion and upgrade decisions. To solve the firm's high-dimensional optimization problem, I develop a reinforcement learning algorithm that decomposes decisions across locations while preserving network-wide strategic coordination. In counterfactual analysis, I study two proposed policy interventions: municipal fiber provision and unbundling schemes where incumbents lease infrastructure access. Municipal broadband expands fiber access by 10% but ultimately reduces total welfare by triggering disinvestment from private competitors. This causes outsized harm to lower income households. Unbundling policies generate more favorable outcomes, particularly for price-sensitive consumers. Under a two-part tariff calibrated to the UK's cost-depreciation-based implementation, consumer surplus increases 12% at the expense of incumbents. I find that when one accounts for firms’ dynamic responses, slashing connection fees while increasing usage fees by half can deliver Pareto improvements and an 18% increase in total surplus.

title: Special Purpose Acquisition Cleantech? Lessons From the Cleantech SPAC Bubble
authors: Will Mosley (Melbourne Business School); David Keith (Melbourne Business School)
abstract: Successful commercialisation of radical clean energy innovation (cleantech) is necessary for the world’s ambitions for net-zero emissions and the Paris Climate targets but venture funding of cleantech start-ups suffers a ‘financial valley of death’ and generates comparably poor returns. In a short-lived ‘Cleantech SPAC bubble’ in 2021, cleantech start-ups merged with special purpose acquisition companies (SPACs) to access $54 billion. Within one year of each merger, SPAC investors had lost on average almost 80% of their investment value. Such losses may be too easy to dismiss, especially as the bubble was co-incident with all-time high trading volumes of dogecoin, non-fungible tokens (NFTs) and shares in GameStop, and Trevor Milton, the high-profile CEO of the cleantech SPAC Nikola, was convicted of fraud. Yet we believe the Cleantech SPAC bubble is worthy of re-examination: why were SPACs one of few real exit opportunities for cleantech start-ups? How did cleantech innovation seemingly find itself with the financial legitimacy of meme coins and Bored Ape NFTs? Cleantech may be more susceptible to speculation, as it has relatively little financial performance data to inform investing. The cleantech SPAC bubble offers a unique opportunity to generate financial performance data, as SPACs have unusual freedom to publicly share forward-looking financial statements. We can evaluate how the forecasts of Cleantech SPACs compare with industrial benchmarks and actual results. In this paper we consider the Cleantech SPAC bubble – its context and its aftermath – and in an analysis of 121 cleantech SPACs, we find that cleantech SPACs significantly exceeded historical benchmark rates of growth and cost reduction, whilst projecting rates of learning well within industry benchmarks. Companies with greater technological maturity and with projections closer to industry benchmarks offered better returns to investors.
